proxy_language: Yoruba (Ife/Oyo-type standard Yoruba) with Edo (Benin) as a secondary check
proxy_rationale: 'The Crossroads Court' is a fictional later court in West Africa with no single historical identity. The crossroads motif (ona-meji, Esu/Eshu as lord of the crossroads) and royal-court institutions point most defensibly to the Yoruba-speaking Ife/Oyo/Benin sphere. Standard Yoruba is richly attested, so it is used as a practical proxy; the link to the fictional culture is weak, hence low confidence. The current game names (Jekgelak, ti, Pafa, Heto) do not look like Yoruba, though 'ti' happens to be a real Yoruba genitive/relative particle.
phonology: Consonants: b t d k g gb (labial-velar stop) kp f s sh [S] h j [dZ] m n l r w y. Vowels: 7 oral i e e-dot [open e] a o o-dot [open o] u, plus nasal vowels written with n (in, an, un, en, on). Three level tones: high (acute), mid (unmarked), low (grave). Vowel harmony in advanced/retracted tongue root appears in prefixes. Nasal consonants m n are syllabic in some words (e.g. n, m as verbal particles).
phonotactics: Syllables are strictly open: V, CV, or syllabic nasal N; no consonant clusters and no word-final consonants. Nasalization is written with a following n only at syllable end (an, en, in, on, un) and counts as part of the vowel. Words are typically 2-4 syllables. Nouns very commonly begin with a vowel (the old noun-class prefix), e.g. oba, ile, omi, eja. Tone is lexical and spelled with diacritics in full orthography.
orthography: Standard Yoruba Latin orthography: letters a b d e (open e with underdot) f g gb h i j k l m n o (open o with underdot) p r s sh (s with underdot) t u w y. Tone marks: acute and grave on vowels (mid unmarked). The letters c q v x z are not used. For the game, the plain-ASCII form (e for open e, o for open o, sh for the dotted s) is acceptable with diacritics optional.
morphology: Isolating-leaning with little inflection. Nouns have no gender, case, or number marking; plurality uses a separate word (awon) or context. Derivation: agentive/nominalizing prefixes a- (one who: alagbede blacksmith, onisowo trader), oni-/ol-/al- (owner of, possessor: oniwa, oloba), ao-/e- abstract (ewa beauty), i- (state/place: ile house, ibi place), o- (agent: oluko teacher). Reduplication creates intensives and nouns. Verbs are bare roots with preverbal particles (ni, ti, yoo, ko).
compounding: Head-initial genitive: possessed noun comes first, possessor second, juxtaposed with no linker (ile oba house of the king; aafin oba palace of the king) or with the linker ti for emphasis/possessive predicates. 'Owner/lord of X' uses oni-/oluwa-/oloh: Olori (head-owner/queen), Oloye (owner of title/chief), Oniona (owner of the road). 'X-maker/seller' uses a-/onI- plus verb or noun: alagbede (one who forges), aroko-ni. Vowel elision/assimilation happens at word boundaries in speech (oba + ile -> obale).
noun_phrase_order: Noun + modifier: noun then possessor, then adjective, then demonstrative/number (omo kekere child small; ile nla house big; ona meji roads two). Genitive: head noun first, possessor after. Names of the type 'Court of the Crossroads' would be aafin + orita (court + crossroads).

Bamgbose, Ayo - A Grammar of Yoruba (1966)
Pulleyblank, D. - Tone in Lexical Phonology (1986)

Ladefoged and Maddieson - The Sounds of the World's Languages (1996), Yoruba section
notes: The Crossroads Court is fictional, so Yoruba is a proxy only; the Edo/Benin and wider Niger-Congo sphere would give similar open-syllable CV phonotactics. Names should be built from real nouns with head-initial genitive order, using oni-/a- prefixes for owner/maker names. Avoid consonant clusters and word-final consonants entirely (the current game strings Jekgelak, Pafa with final -k are not Yoruba-shaped). No word may be identical to a Modern Irish, Scottish Gaelic or Manx word, since Yoruba is not Goidelic; the open-syllable pattern makes accidental overlap unlikely but should still be checked.
